cards.title: What does **Big-O** notation, $O(f(n))$, say about an algorithm's **running time**?
cards.body:
An upper bound on how fast the running time grows with the input size $n$, ignoring constant factors and smaller terms.

An **algorithm** is a step-by-step procedure for a task. Its **running time** is the number of basic steps it takes, written as a function of the input size $n$ (how many items it must handle). Saying the running time is $O(f(n))$ means that, for large enough $n$, it never exceeds a constant multiple of $f(n)$.

Formally: there are constants $c > 0$ and $n_0$ such that running time $\le c \cdot f(n)$ for every $n \ge n_0$.

Example: A routine that takes $3n^2 + 50n + 200$ steps is $O(n^2)$. For large $n$ the $3n^2$ term dwarfs the rest, and the constant 3 is dropped.

Watch out: Big-O is only an upper bound, so a routine that takes $n$ steps is also, truthfully, $O(n^2)$. A bound that is exact needs Big-Theta, covered in the next card.

cards.title: How is **Big-Theta**, $\Theta(f(n))$, defined in terms of Big-O and **Big-Omega**, $\Omega(f(n))$?
cards.body:
$\Theta(f(n))$ means the running time is both $O(f(n))$ and $\Omega(f(n))$: squeezed between constant multiples of $f(n)$, a tight bound.

$\Omega(f(n))$ is the mirror image of Big-O: a lower bound, meaning the running time grows at least as fast as a constant multiple of $f(n)$ for large $n$.

Example: The loop `for (i = 0; i < n; i++) sum += a[i];` takes about $n$ steps, so it is $\Theta(n)$. It is also $O(n^2)$ and $\Omega(1)$, but those statements are true and loose.

Watch out: In everyday speech people say "Big-O" when they mean the tight bound. When it matters, say $\Theta$.

cards.title: Rank these **growth rates** from slowest to fastest: $n^2$, $1$, $2^n$, $n$, $\log n$, $n \log n$.
cards.body:
$1 < \log n < n < n \log n < n^2 < 2^n$

A **growth rate** says how the cost changes as $n$ grows. These six are the ones you meet constantly: constant, logarithmic, linear, $n \log n$, quadratic and exponential.

**Logarithmic time**, $O(\log n)$, means each step cuts the remaining work by a constant fraction, usually in half. Doubling $n$ adds just one more step.

Example: For $n = 1{,}024$:
- $\log_2 n = 10$
- $n = 1{,}024$
- $n \log_2 n = 10{,}240$
- $n^2 = 1{,}048{,}576$
- $2^n \approx 1.8 \times 10^{308}$

Key idea: Doubling $n$ adds one step for $\log n$, doubles the time for $n$, quadruples it for $n^2$ and squares it for $2^n$.

cards.title: Why is it false that **Big-O** and **worst case** mean the same thing?
cards.body:
Worst case chooses which input to measure; Big-O describes how a cost grows. You can state a Big-O bound for the worst case, the best case or the average case.

The **worst case** is the input of a given size that makes the algorithm slowest. Big-O is a way of describing any function, so it can describe the cost on that input or on any other.

Example: Linear search (checking items one by one) takes $O(n)$ steps in the worst case, when the target is last or missing. Its best case, when the target is first, is $O(1)$.

Why it matters: A device with a hard deadline, such as a motor controller, must be sized for the worst case, not the average one.

cards.title: How long is one clock cycle, in nanoseconds, on a core clocked at 100 MHz?
cards.body:
10

The period is the reciprocal of the frequency: $T = 1/f = 1/(10^8\,\mathrm{Hz}) = 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{s} = 10\,\mathrm{ns}$.

Example: If one simple operation took exactly one cycle, a 100 MHz core would do $10^8$ operations per second, $10^5$ per millisecond. A loop of $10^6$ such operations would take $10^6 / 10^8\,\mathrm{s} = 10\,\mathrm{ms}$.

Watch out: One operation per cycle is the best case. A loop iteration usually takes several cycles (load, compare, add, branch), so multiply your operation count by a realistic cycles-per-step figure before dividing by the clock rate.

cards.title: A routine compares every pair of 1,000 sensor readings once (pairs $i < j$). Each comparison costs about 6 clock cycles on a 100 MHz core. Estimate the running time.
cards.body:
About 30 ms.

The number of pairs is $\frac{1000 \cdot 999}{2} = 499{,}500$. At 6 cycles each that is $499{,}500 \times 6 \approx 3.0 \times 10^6$ cycles. At 100 MHz one cycle lasts 10 ns, so the time is $3.0 \times 10^6 \times 10\,\mathrm{ns} \approx 30\,\mathrm{ms}$.

Key idea: Estimate = (operation count) × (cycles per operation) ÷ (clock rate). Loop overhead is ignored here, so treat the result as a rough figure.

Watch out: The count is $\Theta(n^2)$. With 2,000 readings the time would be about four times larger, near 120 ms, which could blow a 100 ms deadline.

cards.title: A routine known to take $\Theta(n \log n)$ time needs 20 ms for $n = 1{,}024$. Estimate its time for $n = 4{,}096$.
cards.body:
About 96 ms.

Work in units of $n \log_2 n$. For $n = 1{,}024$ that is $1{,}024 \times 10 = 10{,}240$. For $n = 4{,}096$ it is $4{,}096 \times 12 = 49{,}152$. The ratio is $49{,}152 / 10{,}240 = 4.8$, so the time is about $20\,\mathrm{ms} \times 4.8 = 96\,\mathrm{ms}$.

Watch out: Making $n$ four times larger does not make the time four times larger (that would be 80 ms for a linear routine), and certainly not sixteen times larger (320 ms for a quadratic one). The $\log n$ factor adds a little.

Tip: Scaling from a measured time like this cancels the unknown constant factor, which is why measuring one run beats guessing cycle counts.

cards.title: On a microcontroller, when can a plain $O(n^2)$ routine beat an $O(n \log n)$ one?
cards.body:
When $n$ is small: constant factors then dominate, so a simple quadratic routine can be faster than a more elaborate $n \log n$ one.

Example: Suppose routine A takes $3n^2$ steps and routine B takes $40\,n \log_2 n$ steps. At $n = 50$ A needs 7,500 steps and B about 11,300. They cross near $n = 85$; beyond that B wins, and at $n = 1{,}000$ A needs 3,000,000 steps against about 400,000 for B.

Why it matters: On a microcontroller the simple routine is often also smaller in code, needs no extra RAM and has no deep recursion. If $n$ is guaranteed small (say at most a few dozen), it is often the right pick.

Watch out: The other side is that $n$ tends to grow later. If the limit on $n$ isn't enforced by design, choose the routine whose growth rate stays safe.

cards.title: What is **cache locality**, and what **memory hierarchy** makes it matter?
cards.body:
Cache locality is touching data that sits close together in memory or was used recently, so the small, fast memories near the processor can serve it.

The **memory hierarchy** is a stack of memories: registers, then caches (small, fast copies of recently used memory), then main RAM, then flash or storage. Each level down is bigger and slower. When the processor reads one byte, the cache fetches a whole **cache line** around it, commonly 32 or 64 bytes.

Example: Walking an `int32_t` array front to back, one cache line brings in 8 or 16 items at once, so most reads are served from the cache. Following list pointers to nodes scattered around the heap can cost a fresh trip to slower memory for every item.

Why it matters: At 45 nm, Horowitz (ISSCC 2014) puts a 32-bit read at about 5 pJ from an 8 KB SRAM and about 640 pJ from DRAM, so misses cost energy as well as time.

Watch out: Many small microcontrollers, such as Cortex-M0 or M4 parts, have no data cache at all. There locality matters less, but larger cores (the Cortex-M7 has optional caches) and every application processor depend on it.

cards.title: Why is appending to a **dynamic array** that doubles its capacity **amortised** $O(1)$, even though a single append can cost $O(n)$?
cards.body:
Each doubling copies at most $n$ items, but it happens only after about $n$ cheap appends, so the average cost per append stays constant.

A **dynamic array** is an array with a `size` (items stored) and a `capacity` (slots allocated). When it is full, you allocate double the capacity, copy the items over and free the old block (`realloc` does this).

**Amortised cost** is the average cost per operation over a whole sequence of operations, taken in the worst case. It is not an average over random inputs.

Why it works: Doubling from capacity 1, the copies happen at sizes $1, 2, 4, \dots, n/2$, which add up to $n - 1$, fewer than the $n$ appends that caused them. That is about two item writes per append.

Watch out: Growing by a fixed amount (say 4 slots) instead of doubling makes the total copying quadratic, so appends become $O(n)$ amortised.

cards.title: A dynamic array of `int32_t` starts with capacity 8 and doubles when full. Over 100 appends, how many elements are copied in total by all the growths?
cards.body:
120 elements (8 + 16 + 32 + 64).

The array grows when an append finds it full. That happens at the 9th append (size 8, copy 8 items into a block of 16), the 17th (copy 16 into 32), the 33rd (copy 32 into 64) and the 65th (copy 64 into 128). Capacity 128 then covers appends up to the 128th, so there are no more growths by 100.

Total copies: $8 + 16 + 32 + 64 = 120$, about 1.2 copies per append: this is the amortised $O(1)$ cost in numbers.

Example: At 4 bytes per item the final block is $128 \times 4 = 512$ bytes, of which 400 are in use.

Watch out: During the last growth `realloc` may need the old 256-byte block and the new 512-byte block at the same time, so the heap needs 768 bytes free. Doubling is cheap in time, but it needs RAM headroom.

cards.title: You must store 500 sensor readings (`int32_t`) on a 32-bit Cortex-M. You read them by index and scan them in order, with only an occasional insert in the middle. **Array or linked list?**
cards.body:
An array.

- **Access by index:** array $O(1)$, list $O(n)$ (follow pointers).
- **Insert in the middle:** array $O(n)$ (shift later items), list $O(1)$ once you hold the node, but finding it is $O(n)$.
- **Memory:** array 4 bytes per reading, 2,000 bytes in all; list 8 bytes per node (4 for the value, 4 for the pointer), 4,000 bytes, plus whatever bookkeeping the allocator adds for each `malloc`.
- **Scanning:** the array is contiguous, so it has far better cache locality.

Example: Shifting 500 readings to make room for one is a single block copy of at most 2,000 bytes, a trivial cost for an occasional insert.

Watch out: The other side: a linked list wins when you insert or remove at known positions all the time, when items are large and must not be moved, or when pointers to items must stay valid. Without those needs, the array's compactness and speed usually decide it.

cards.title: A microcontroller with 32 KiB of RAM receives at most 64 samples per frame. Should the code use a dynamic array or a fixed-size array?
cards.body:
A fixed-size array of 64 samples, sized for the worst case.

It never calls `malloc` or `realloc`, so there is no allocation failure at run time, no fragmentation and no timing jitter from the allocator. The linker's map shows exactly how much RAM it costs: $64 \times 4 = 256$ bytes for `int32_t` samples.

Why it matters: Firmware that must run for months can't afford a rare out-of-memory failure that only shows up in the field.

Watch out: The price is wasted space when frames are usually shorter, and a hard limit: sample 65 has nowhere to go, so the code must decide what to do (drop it, flag an error). A dynamic array wins when the maximum is unknown and RAM is plentiful, as on a Linux-class system.

cards.title: What is a **stack** (as a data structure), and what does **LIFO** stand for?
cards.body:
A stack holds items so that the last one pushed is the first one popped: last in, first out (**LIFO**).

You have two main operations, `push` (add on top) and `pop` (remove from the top), and both take $O(1)$ time on an array with a `top` index:

```c
st[top++] = x;     /* push */
x = st[--top];     /* pop  */
```

Example: An undo history is a stack: the most recent edit is the first one undone.

Watch out: Check for overflow (`top == capacity`) before pushing and for underflow (`top == 0`) before popping. Don't confuse this data structure with the call stack in memory: that one is a stack too (each call pushes a frame, each return pops it), but here we mean a stack you build and manage yourself.

cards.title: What is a **queue**, and what does **FIFO** mean?
cards.body:
A queue gives items back in the order they arrived: first in, first out (**FIFO**).

The two operations are `enqueue` (add at the back) and `dequeue` (remove from the front).

Example: Bytes arriving on a serial port wait in a queue until the program is ready for them, and the oldest byte must be handled first.

Watch out: A queue built on a plain array that shifts every item forward on each dequeue costs $O(n)$ per dequeue. Moving the front index forward instead leaves empty space at the start, and the next cards show how a ring buffer reuses it.

cards.title: What is a **ring buffer** (circular buffer), and what do its **head index** and **tail index** do?
cards.body:
A ring buffer is a fixed-size array used as a queue: items are written at the head index and read from the tail index, and both indices wrap around to 0 at the end of the array.

Convention used here: `head` is where the next item will be written, and `tail` is where the next item will be read. Some code bases swap these names, so check before reading someone else's code.

```c
buf[head] = x;  head = (head + 1) % N;   /* write */
x = buf[tail];  tail = (tail + 1) % N;   /* read  */
```

Why: Nothing is ever shifted. A read frees the slot at the tail, and the head will reach that slot again after wrapping around. Read and write are both $O(1)$ and the memory use is fixed.

Example: A receive buffer for a serial port is a ring buffer: the hardware side fills it and your code drains it.

cards.title: A ring buffer has $N = 8$ slots and keeps one slot unused so that its **full** and **empty** conditions can be told apart. If `head = 2` and `tail = 3`, how many items does it hold, and is it full?
cards.body:
It holds 7 items and is full.

- **Empty:** `head == tail`.
- **Full:** `(head + 1) % N == tail`. Here $(2 + 1) \bmod 8 = 3 = \text{tail}$, so it is full.
- **Count:** $(\text{head} - \text{tail}) \bmod N = (2 - 3) \bmod 8 = 7$.

Why one slot is sacrificed: If all $N$ slots could be filled, a full buffer would have `head == tail`, exactly like an empty one. Giving up one slot makes the two cases differ. The usable capacity is $N - 1$.

Watch out: In C, `(head - tail) % N` is negative when `head < tail` and the indices are signed. Write `(head - tail + N) % N`, or use unsigned indices. Another way out is to keep a separate item count.

Two `get` calls return 10 and then 20, so `v` ends as 20 and `tail` is 2. Now `put(60)` finds a free slot (`head` moves from 3 to 0, which is not `tail`) and succeeds: 4 successes in total.

cards.title: Why does a **ring buffer** with one **producer** and one **consumer** suit passing data from an interrupt to the main loop?
cards.body:
Each index has exactly one writer (the interrupt handler writes `head`, the main loop writes `tail`), so no lock is needed.

An **interrupt** is a hardware event that pauses the main code, runs a short function (an interrupt service routine, ISR) and then resumes the main code. In this **producer–consumer** pattern the ISR is the producer (it makes data) and the main loop is the consumer (it uses it).

The rules:
- The producer writes the item into the slot, then advances `head`.
- The consumer reads the item from the slot, then advances `tail`.
- Both indices are declared `volatile`, since the other side changes them behind the compiler's back.

Why: The consumer never sees a half-written item, because `head` moves only after the data is in place.

Watch out: This holds for one producer and one consumer on a single core. Several producers, or a second processor core, need extra care.

cards.body:
Declare `head` as `volatile`: `static volatile uint8_t head;`. Without it the compiler may read `head` once and spin forever.

Nothing in `main_get` changes `head`, so an optimizing compiler may load it once before the loop. On a 64-bit Arm host at `-O2` this code compiles to a loop that never reads `head` again, an infinite loop. `volatile` forces a fresh read on every pass.

Key idea: The interrupt runs outside the normal flow of the main code, so the compiler can't see the change. Any variable shared with an ISR and polled in a loop needs `volatile`.

cards.title: A serial link delivers 11,520 bytes per second. The main loop can be busy for up to 20 ms before it empties the buffer. What is the smallest power-of-two size, in bytes, for a ring buffer that keeps one slot unused and never overflows?
cards.body:
256

In 20 ms the link delivers $11{,}520 \times 0.020 = 230.4$ bytes, so up to 231 bytes can arrive while the main loop is busy. With one slot unused a buffer of $N$ slots holds $N - 1$ items, so $N - 1 \ge 231$, giving $N \ge 232$. The next power of two is $N = 256$.

Example: 11,520 bytes per second is a serial line at 115,200 bits per second with 10 bits on the wire per byte (8 data bits plus a start and a stop bit).

Why it matters: A buffer of 128 would overflow after about 11 ms of delay ($127 / 11{,}520 \approx 11\,\mathrm{ms}$), so the choice depends directly on the worst-case delay.

Tip: Size from the worst delay you can measure, then add margin. Here 256 leaves 24 spare bytes.

cards.title: Interrupt-driven firmware must queue incoming messages. Which is the better default: a fixed-size ring buffer, or a linked-list queue with one `malloc`ed node per message?
cards.body:
A fixed-size ring buffer, when the number of queued messages has a known bound and the code runs in an interrupt.

- It takes fixed RAM, visible at link time.
- Put and get are $O(1)$ with predictable timing.
- No heap, so no allocation failure and no fragmentation.

`malloc` inside an interrupt handler is a poor idea: the call can be slow, its timing varies, it can return `NULL`, and common allocators aren't safe to call while main code may be inside them.

Watch out: A ring buffer forces you to decide what happens when it is full (drop the new item or overwrite the oldest). A linked-list queue wins when messages vary a lot in size, when there is no sensible bound, or when items must move between queues without copying, and when the code runs on a system with a real allocator and enough RAM.

cards.title: What is a **hash function**, and what two properties make it good for a table?
cards.body:
A hash function turns a key into an integer, which is then reduced to a table index. A good one gives the same result for the same key every time and spreads different keys evenly.

Typical use: `index = hash(key) % N`, where $N$ is the number of slots in the table.

Example: A common simple string hash starts with `h = 5381` and, for each character `c`, sets `h = h * 33 + c`. Every character changes the whole value, so "stop" and "pots", which have the same letters, still get different hash values.

Why: If the function wasn't deterministic you could never find a key again. If it spreads keys unevenly, many keys pile into a few slots and the table becomes slow.

Watch out: The cost of hashing is $O(\text{length of the key})$, not $O(1)$. Hashing a long string for every lookup adds up.

cards.title: What is a **hash table**, and what is a **bucket**?
cards.body:
A hash table is an array of buckets in which each key is stored at the index its hash function gives, so lookup and insert take $O(1)$ time on average.

A **bucket** is one slot of that array. Depending on the design it holds one item or a chain of items.

Lookup in three steps: hash the key, reduce it to an index, check that bucket.

Example: With 8 buckets, a key whose hash reduces to index 3 is stored and later looked up in bucket 3, without looking at the other seven.

Watch out: "$O(1)$ on average" assumes the keys spread well. If everything lands in one bucket, a lookup degrades to $O(n)$.

cards.title: What is a **collision** in a hash table, and why can't you avoid collisions entirely?
cards.body:
A collision is two different keys landing in the same bucket. When there are more possible keys than buckets, some collisions must happen.

Example: With 4 buckets and `index = key % 4`, the keys 5 and 13 both land in bucket 1.

Even with few keys, collisions come sooner than most people expect: 23 random keys in 365 buckets already have about a 50% chance that at least two share a bucket (the birthday problem).

Key idea: Every hash table needs a collision strategy. The two classic ones are **separate chaining** (each bucket holds a list of its items) and **linear probing** (on a collision, try the following slots one by one). The next cards show both.

Key idea: A lookup costs the length of one chain, about $1 + \alpha$ steps on average for load factor $\alpha$ (items per bucket). Chains can grow past one item per bucket, so the table never "fills up".

Tip: Deleting is easy: unlink the node from its chain, just as in an ordinary linked list.

At the 13th insertion; 12 keys are reinserted into a table of 32 slots.

After 12 keys the load factor is $12/16 = 0.75$, which is not above the limit, so the 12th insertion goes ahead. The 13th would make $13/16 = 0.8125 > 0.75$, so the table is rebuilt first.

Why every key is reinserted: Each key's slot is `hash % size`. When the size changes from 16 to 32, the same hash gives a different index, so copying the old array in place would leave keys where lookups no longer look.

Example: After the rehash the 13 keys sit in 32 slots, a load factor of about 0.41.

Linear probing in a fixed array, keeping the load factor at or below roughly 0.5 to 0.7.

- No per-item allocation and no pointers: an entry is just a slot, with 4 fewer bytes of overhead per item on a 32-bit target.
- Slots are contiguous, so probing is cache-friendly.
- RAM use is known at link time.

Probing gets slow as the table fills (see the load factor card: about 8.5 probes for a miss at 0.75), so you must leave free slots and cap the number of items.

A sorted `const` array searched by binary search.

- The table sits in flash and uses no RAM.
- There is no hash function, no collision handling and no resizing; a build script can sort it.

The plain array is simplest, but scanning averages about 20 string comparisons and worst case 40. A hash table needs space for buckets and code to build it.

cards.title: What is **binary search**, what must be true of its input, and what does it cost?
cards.body:
Binary search finds a target in a sorted array by comparing it with the middle item and discarding the half that cannot hold it; it needs sorted input and takes $O(\log n)$ comparisons.

The alternative is **linear search**: check items one by one from the start. It works on unsorted data but takes $O(n)$ comparisons in the worst case.

Example: For $n = 1{,}000{,}000$ items, binary search needs at most $\lfloor \log_2 10^6 \rfloor + 1 = 20$ comparisons; linear search may need a million.

Watch out: On unsorted data binary search silently returns wrong answers, because discarding a half is only valid when the order guarantees the target isn't there. If you sort first, sorting costs $O(n \log n)$, so it only pays off when you search many times.

cards.title: What is a **stable sort**?
cards.body:
A sort that keeps items with equal keys in the same relative order they had in the input.

Example: Sort these (name, score) records by score: (Ann, 90), (Bo, 85), (Cy, 90). A stable sort outputs Bo 85, Ann 90, Cy 90: Ann still comes before Cy. An unstable sort might output Cy before Ann.

Why it matters: Stability lets you sort by several keys in turn. Sort by the minor key (name) first, then sort by the major key (score) with a stable sort, and ties on score remain ordered by name.

Watch out: Insertion sort and merge sort are stable when written to keep equal items in order; common quicksort and heapsort implementations are not. The C library's `qsort` makes no promise of stability.

cards.title: What is an **in-place sort**, and why does it matter on a microcontroller?
cards.body:
A sort that rearranges the items inside the original array, using only a small, fixed amount of extra memory that doesn't grow with $n$.

Insertion sort and heapsort are in place. Merge sort is normally not: it needs a second array of $n$ items to merge into. Quicksort is usually called in place, although its recursion uses stack space (about $\log n$ levels when the smaller part is handled first).

Example: Sorting 2,000 `int16_t` samples (4,000 bytes) with merge sort needs another 4,000 bytes of buffer. An in-place sort needs almost none.

Why it matters: RAM is the scarce resource on a microcontroller, and a buffer the size of the data can be the difference between fitting and not fitting.

On already sorted input the `while` test fails at once every time: zero shifts, and the whole sort takes $\Theta(n)$ steps. That is the best case.

cards.title: Quicksort takes the last item of each range as its pivot, and partitioning a range of $m$ items makes $m - 1$ comparisons with the pivot. How many comparisons does it make in total on an array of 1,000 items that is already sorted?

499,500

On sorted input the pivot is always the largest item of its range, so partition puts it at the end and the "after" part is empty. A range of $m$ items costs $m - 1$ comparisons and leaves a range of $m - 1$ items to sort. The total is $999 + 998 + \dots + 1 = \frac{1000 \cdot 999}{2} = 499{,}500$, the same as insertion sort's worst case: $\Theta(n^2)$.

Why it matters on a small device: The recursion also goes about 1,000 calls deep, one stack frame each. A stack of a few KiB can overflow.

Tip: Real implementations avoid this by picking the pivot better (the median of three items, or a random one) and by recursing into the smaller part first, which caps the depth at about $\log_2 n$. The average cost of quicksort is $O(n \log n)$.

For $n = 1{,}024$, each item is copied once per merging level. At 8 cycles per copy on a 100 MHz core, about how long do the copies take?

About 0.82 ms.

Halving 1,024 items down to single items takes $\log_2 1024 = 10$ levels, and every level copies all 1,024 items once: $10 \times 1{,}024 = 10{,}240$ copies. At 8 cycles each that is $81{,}920$ cycles, and at 10 ns per cycle, $0.82\,\mathrm{ms}$.

Example: Merging 2, 7, 9 with 3, 4: compare the fronts 2 and 3, take 2; 7 and 3, take 3; 7 and 4, take 4; the second half is empty, so copy the rest, 7 and 9. The result is 2 3 4 7 9 after 3 comparisons (at most $3 + 2 - 1 = 4$).

Watch out: Merging needs a spare array as long as the data (2 KiB for 1,024 `int16_t` values), so merge sort is not in place. Its worst case is $O(n \log n)$, with no bad inputs like quicksort has, and it is stable.

cards.title: Why must any **comparison-based sort** make at least about $n \log_2 n$ comparisons in the worst case? (This is the **comparison-sort lower bound**.)
cards.body:
$\Omega(n \log n)$: there are $n!$ possible orderings of $n$ items and each comparison gives one yes-or-no answer, so at least $\log_2(n!) \approx n \log_2 n$ comparisons are needed.

Here $n! = n \times (n-1) \times \dots \times 1$ counts the ways to order $n$ distinct items. A sort has to work out which of them it was given. Each comparison can at best halve the set of orderings still possible, so it needs at least $\log_2(n!)$ comparisons to get down to one.

Example: For $n = 10$ there are $10! = 3{,}628{,}800$ orderings, and $\log_2 3{,}628{,}800 \approx 21.8$, so at least 22 comparisons are needed in the worst case.

Watch out: The bound only covers sorts that learn about the order by comparing two items. A sort that uses the key values directly, such as counting sort, can beat it.

Counting sort: tally how many times each value occurs in 256 counters, then write the values out in order. It takes $O(n + k)$ time for $k = 256$ possible values.

Cost: about $10{,}000 + 256$ steps per pass, against roughly $n \log_2 n \approx 132{,}900$ comparisons for a comparison sort. The counters need $256 \times 2 = 512$ bytes (`uint16_t`, since counts reach 10,000).

Why it works: The value itself is used as an index into the counter array, so no comparisons are made. This is how it gets under the $n \log n$ bound.

Watch out: The other side: counting sort needs the key range $k$ to be small. For 32-bit keys it would need $2^{32}$ counters, and a comparison sort wins easily. Sorting records by a key (not just the values) also needs an output array of $n$ items to stay stable.

Insertion sort: it is in place, stable, needs no recursion and very little code, and for 12 values it does at most $12 \cdot 11 / 2 = 66$ shifts.

Merge sort would need a second array of 12 items and extra code, and its $n \log n$ advantage hardly shows at this size, where simple loops and small constants decide the cost.

cards.title: What is a **tree**, and what are its **root**, **leaf** and **height**?
cards.body:
A tree is a set of nodes joined by parent-to-child links: one **root** has no parent, every other node has exactly one parent, a **leaf** has no children, and the **height** is the number of links on the longest path from the root down to a leaf.

Example: A folder structure is a tree. The top folder is the root, files and empty folders are leaves, and the height is how many folder levels you cross to reach the deepest file.

Convention used in the next cards: a tree with a single node has height 0, and an empty tree has height $-1$.

Why it matters: The height controls the cost of most tree operations, because they walk down one root-to-leaf path. A tree that holds $n$ nodes and gives each node at most two children can be as short as about $\log_2 n$ or as tall as $n - 1$.

cards.title: What is a **binary search tree** (BST), and what rule does it keep?
cards.body:
A tree in which each node has at most two children (left and right), and every key in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node's key while every key in its right subtree is larger.

A **subtree** is a node together with everything below it. The rule is about the whole subtree, not just the immediate children.

Why: A search compares the target with the current key and discards one whole subtree, the way binary search discards half of an array. A search takes $O(h)$ steps for a tree of height $h$.

Watch out: A tree where 50 has the left child 30, and 30 has the right child 60, breaks the rule: 60 is greater than 30, but it sits in the left subtree of 50 and so must be less than 50. Checking only parent and child misses this. Duplicate keys need a stated policy; the code in the following cards ignores them.

cards.title: Why does a plain BST degrade to $O(n)$ when keys arrive in sorted order, and what does a **balanced tree** such as a **red-black tree** guarantee?
cards.body:
Sorted inserts build a chain of height $n - 1$, so search is $O(n)$. A balanced tree keeps its height $O(\log n)$ by rearranging nodes as it grows; a red-black tree's height is at most $2\log_2(n+1)$.

A **balanced tree** is one whose height is kept close to the minimum, about $\log_2 n$. A **red-black tree** is a BST in which every node is colored red or black under rules that stop any root-to-leaf path from being more than twice as long as another. Insert and delete restore the rules by recolouring and by rotations (local rearrangements that keep the BST order). Search, insert and delete are all $O(\log n)$ in the worst case.

Example: For $n = 1{,}000{,}000$ keys, a chain needs up to a million steps for a search. A red-black tree's height is at most $2 \log_2(1{,}000{,}001) \approx 39.9$, so at most 39.

Why it matters: Balanced trees are the standard sorted-map structure (C++'s `std::map` is commonly a red-black tree), but they are rarely worth their code size on a small device; a sorted array is often enough.

(a) No: the chain is 100 nodes deep, so it needs $100 \times 32 = 3{,}200$ bytes, more than the 2,048 available. (b) Yes: a perfectly balanced tree of 1,023 keys has 10 levels, so it needs $10 \times 32 = 320$ bytes.

The stack holds 2,048 / 32 = 64 frames at most. Sorted insertion makes a chain with 100 levels, which overflows it, and the device crashes or corrupts memory.

Why it matters: Stack use grows with the height of the tree. Keep the tree balanced, or avoid recursion: loops for search and insert use constant stack, and an explicit, bounded stack of your own handles a traversal.

Hash table. A trie node costs 108 bytes on a 32-bit target, and words share memory only through common prefixes.

The size: $26 \times 4 = 104$ bytes of pointers plus 1 byte for the flag is 105, padded to 108 so the struct stays 4-byte aligned. In practice most nodes have only a few real children, so most of those 26 slots are wasted `NULL` pointers.

What the trie offers: lookup takes $O(\text{word length})$ steps no matter how many words are stored, there are no hash collisions, and finding every word with a given prefix (autocomplete) is natural.

Watch out: The other side: when RAM is plentiful, or prefix queries matter, a trie is a good fit. Compressed variants that merge single-child chains cut the waste, at the price of more complex code. In a hash table the cost is about one small node (or one slot) per word.

cards.title: What is the **heap property**, and how does a **min-heap** differ from a **max-heap**?
cards.body:
In a binary heap, every node is ordered against its children: in a **min-heap** each parent is at most both its children (the smallest key is at the root); in a **max-heap** each parent is at least both children (the largest is at the root).

A **binary heap** is a tree with at most two children per node, filled level by level from left to right with no gaps, and obeying the heap property.

Example: $[1, 3, 8, 5, 9, 10]$ is a min-heap: 1 is below both 3 and 8, 3 is below 5 and 9, and 8 is below 10.

Watch out: A heap is not sorted. Siblings have no order (3 and 8 above), and it is not a binary search tree: left does not mean smaller. Only the root's value is known to be the smallest (or largest). Also, this "heap" is not the memory heap that `malloc` uses; the names just coincide.

cards.title: What is a **priority queue**, and what operations does it support?
cards.body:
A priority queue is a collection from which you always remove the item with the highest priority (for example, the smallest deadline): operations are `insert` and `extract-min` (or `extract-max`).

Unlike a FIFO queue, the order of removal depends on the items' priorities, not on when they arrived.

Why it matters: A binary heap implements it so that both operations take $O(\log n)$ time. A sorted array makes extraction fast but insertion $O(n)$, and an unsorted array makes insertion fast but extraction $O(n)$.

Example: A scheduler keeps the pending timers in a priority queue keyed by deadline, so the next timer to fire is always the root.

cards.title: How is a binary heap stored in an array, and where are the children and parent of index $i$?
cards.body:
Level by level in a plain array (indexed from 0): the children of index $i$ are at $2i + 1$ and $2i + 2$, and its parent is at $\lfloor (i - 1)/2 \rfloor$.

Because the heap is filled without gaps, no pointers are needed: position alone says who is whose child. A heap of $n$ items has height $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$.

Example: In $[1, 3, 8, 5, 9, 10]$, index 1 (value 3) has children at indices 3 and 4 (values 5 and 9), and index 5 (value 10) has parent $\lfloor 4/2 \rfloor = 2$ (value 8). With $n = 6$ the height is $\lfloor \log_2 6 \rfloor = 2$.

Tip: The last index that has a child is $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor - 1$ (here 2); every index after it is a leaf.

Watch out: Many textbooks index from 1, with children at $2i$ and $2i + 1$. With C arrays starting at 0, use the 0-based formulas.

The 10 ms timer fires first; afterwards the array is $[20, 40, 30, 50]$.

Inserts (sift-up each time): 40 gives $[40]$; 10 swaps with 40: $[10, 40]$; 30 stays: $[10, 40, 30]$; 20 sits at index 3 under 40 and swaps: $[10, 20, 30, 40]$, and 10 is smaller than 20, so it stops; 50 stays at index 4 under 20: $[10, 20, 30, 40, 50]$.

Extract-min: remove 10, move the last item 50 to the root: $[50, 20, 30, 40]$. Sift-down: the smaller child of the root is 20, swap: $[20, 50, 30, 40]$. Index 1 has the child 40 (index 3), smaller than 50, swap: $[20, 40, 30, 50]$.

Why it matters: A heap gives the next deadline in $O(1)$ (it is the root) and updates in $O(\log n)$, whereas scanning an unsorted list of timers for the earliest costs $O(n)$ on every tick.

cards.title: What is **heapsort**, and what does it cost?
cards.body:
Heapsort builds a max-heap in the array, then repeatedly swaps the root (the largest item) with the last item of the heap, shrinks the heap by one and sifts the new root down: $O(n \log n)$ worst case, in place, not stable.

1. Build a max-heap by sifting down from index $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor - 1$ back to 0; this takes $O(n)$.
2. Swap the root with the last heap item; the largest is now in its final place at the end.
3. Shrink the heap by one and sift the new root down; this takes $O(\log n)$.
4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until the heap is empty.

Why it matters: It combines a guaranteed $O(n \log n)$ worst case with no extra memory, unlike merge sort (needs a buffer) and quicksort (bad worst case).

Watch out: Heapsort jumps around the array (parent and child can be far apart), so it has poor cache locality, and it is usually slower than quicksort on large data.

cards.title: The array $[9, 6, 8, 2, 5, 7]$ is a max-heap. Heapsort performs two steps (each: swap the root with the last heap item, shrink the heap, sift down the root). What is the array after the second step?
cards.body:
$[7, 6, 5, 2, 8, 9]$

Step 1: swap the root 9 with the last item 7: $[7, 6, 8, 2, 5 \mid 9]$ (the bar separates the sorted tail). Sift 7 down in the heap of 5 items: its children are 6 and 8, the larger is 8, swap: $[8, 6, 7, 2, 5 \mid 9]$.

Step 2: swap the root 8 with the last heap item 5: $[5, 6, 7, 2 \mid 8, 9]$. Sift 5 down in the heap of 4 items: children 6 and 7, the larger is 7, swap: $[7, 6, 5, 2 \mid 8, 9]$. The children of index 2 would be at index 5 or beyond, outside the heap, so it stops.

Key idea: Each step moves the largest remaining item to its final position at the end, so after $k$ steps the last $k$ slots hold the $k$ largest items in order.

Tip: In a max-heap sift-down, swap with the larger child. In the min-heap of the previous cards it was the smaller one.

cards.title: What is a **graph**, and what are its **vertices** and **edges**?
cards.body:
A graph is a set of vertices (the things) and edges (links between pairs of vertices); edges are either undirected (a two-way link) or directed (an arrow from one vertex to another).

Written $V$ for the number of vertices and $E$ for the number of edges. With no self-links, an undirected graph has at most $V(V-1)/2$ edges and a directed graph at most $V(V-1)$.

Example: Radio nodes in a mesh are vertices and the radio links between them are undirected edges. The layers of a neural network are vertices and "layer A feeds layer B" is a directed edge.

Why it matters: A tree is a special graph too: undirected, with no way to walk around in a loop. Graphs are the general tool for dependencies, networks and maps.

cards.title: What are an **adjacency list** and an **adjacency matrix**?
cards.body:
An adjacency list stores, for each vertex, the list of its neighbors (memory $O(V + E)$); an adjacency matrix is a $V \times V$ table whose entry $(u, v)$ says whether an edge from $u$ to $v$ exists (memory $O(V^2)$).

Example: For the undirected graph with edges 0–1, 0–2 and 1–2:
- list: `0: {1, 2}`, `1: {0, 2}`, `2: {0, 1}`
- matrix: row 0 is `0 1 1`, row 1 is `1 0 1`, row 2 is `1 1 0`

Costs: the matrix answers "is there an edge from $u$ to $v$?" in $O(1)$. The list lists all the neighbors of $u$ in time proportional to their number, and uses far less memory when edges are few.

Tip: On a microcontroller both are often plain static arrays: a matrix as a 2-D array (or bits), a list as arrays of neighbor indices.

cards.title: What is a **topological sort**, and which graphs have one?
cards.body:
A topological sort orders the vertices of a directed graph so that every edge $u \to v$ has $u$ before $v$; one exists exactly when the graph is a **directed acyclic graph** (DAG), meaning it has no directed cycle.

A cycle is a path that leads back to its starting vertex by following arrows.

Example: Build dependencies. If `app` is linked from `a.o` and `b.o`, and each `.o` is compiled from its `.c` file, an edge goes from each prerequisite to the thing that needs it. A topological order is a valid build order, such as `a.c, b.c, a.o, b.o, app`.

Watch out: A DAG usually has many valid orders. And a cycle (A needs B, B needs A) has none: that is how a topological sort detects circular dependencies.

cards.title: How do **breadth-first search** (BFS) and **depth-first search** (DFS) differ in the order they visit vertices?
cards.body:
BFS visits vertices in order of their distance from the start, using a queue; DFS follows one path as deep as it can before backing up, using recursion (a stack).

Both mark each vertex as visited, so every reachable vertex is processed once. With an adjacency list both take $O(V + E)$ time.

BFS in an unweighted graph finds the path with the fewest edges to every vertex. DFS is the basis of cycle detection and of one way to compute a topological order.

Watch out: Without the visited mark, a graph with a cycle would make either search loop forever.

Watch out: DFS recursion can go as deep as the number of vertices. On a device with a small stack, use an explicit, bounded stack or limit the graph size.

cards.body:
`0 1 2 4 3`

The queue starts as $[0]$. Vertex 0 is removed and its unseen neighbors 1 and 2 are added: $[1, 2]$. Vertex 1 adds 4: $[2, 4]$. Vertex 2 adds 3: $[4, 3]$. Then 4 and 3 are removed, adding nothing new. So the order is 0, then its neighbors 1 and 2, then their new neighbors 4 and 3.

Key idea: Mark a vertex as seen when it is added to the queue, not when it is removed. Otherwise a vertex can be queued several times.

Why: Each vertex enters the queue at most once, so an array of $V$ entries is enough and never needs to wrap around. With a matrix the scan for neighbors makes the whole search $O(V^2)$.

cards.body:
`0 1 4 3 2`

DFS goes from 0 to its first neighbor 1, then from 1 to its first unseen neighbor 4 (0 is already seen), then from 4 to 3, then from 3 to 2. Vertex 2 has no unseen neighbors, so the calls unwind: 3, 4, 1 and finally 0 find nothing more, and the search ends.

Compare BFS on the same graph, which printed `0 1 2 4 3`: BFS fans out from 0 in layers, while DFS dives down one path first.

Watch out: Each recursive call uses a stack frame, so the depth can reach $V$ on a long chain. The `seen` array both stops cycles from looping and keeps the cost at $O(V + E)$.

cards.title: A small network has these data dependencies: `input → convA`, `input → convB`, `convA → concat`, `convB → concat`, `concat → out`. Give one valid execution order for its layers. How many valid orders exist?
cards.body:
`input, convA, convB, concat, out`; there are exactly 2 valid orders, because `convA` and `convB` may run in either order.

The rule is that each layer runs after every layer that feeds it, which is a topological sort of the layer graph. `input` has to come first and `out` last, and `concat` needs both branches finished.

Why it matters: An inference engine needs such an order before it can run a network layer by layer. The choice also affects memory: after `convA` its output must stay alive until `concat` runs, so it sits in RAM while `convB` executes.

Tip: On a straight chain of layers there is only one valid order. Branches and skip connections are what create several, and the engine can pick the one that needs the least RAM.

cards.body:
`3 5 1 0 4 2`

In-degrees: vertex 0 has 1 (from 5), vertex 1 has 1, vertex 2 has 2, vertex 3 has 0, vertex 4 has 2 and vertex 5 has 0. The queue starts as $[3, 5]$.

Remove 3: vertex 1 drops to 0 and is queued; 4 drops to 1. Remove 5: vertex 0 drops to 0 and is queued. Remove 1: vertex 2 drops to 1. Remove 0: vertex 4 drops to 0 and is queued. Remove 4: vertex 2 drops to 0 and is queued. Remove 2. The order is 3, 5, 1, 0, 4, 2, and every edge points forward in it.

Key idea: A vertex with in-degree 0 has nothing left to wait for, so it is safe to output next.

Watch out: Scanning all $E$ edges for each vertex makes this $O(V \cdot E)$. With adjacency lists, Kahn's algorithm takes $O(V + E)$.

cards.body:
`1 of 4: cycle`

In-degrees: vertex 0 has 0, vertex 1 has 2 (from 0 and 2), vertex 2 has 1 and vertex 3 has 1. Only vertex 0 starts in the queue. Removing it lowers vertex 1 from 2 to 1, not to 0, so nothing new is queued and the loop ends with `tail = 1`, which is less than $V = 4$.

Why: Vertices 1 and 2 form a cycle (1→2→1). Each waits for the other, so neither ever reaches in-degree 0, and 3 is stuck behind 2.

Key idea: A directed graph is a DAG exactly when Kahn's algorithm outputs all $V$ vertices. In a build system or a layer graph, this is how a circular dependency gets reported.

cards.title: A mesh of six radio nodes has the links 0–1, 0–2, 1–3, 2–3, 3–4, 4–5 and 2–5. What is the fewest number of hops (links) a message needs from node 0 to node 4?
cards.body:
3

Run BFS from node 0 and group the vertices by layer. Layer 0 is $\{0\}$. Layer 1 holds the neighbors of 0: $\{1, 2\}$. Layer 2 holds the new neighbors of those: node 3 (via 1 or 2) and node 5 (via 2), so $\{3, 5\}$. Layer 3 holds node 4 (via 3 or 5). Node 4 is in layer 3, so 3 hops.

Why it works: BFS reaches vertices in order of increasing distance, so the first time it discovers a vertex, it did so along a shortest path. Recording the layer number (or the parent) of each vertex gives distances and routes.

Watch out: This works for unweighted graphs, where every hop counts the same. If links have different costs (energy, delay), a different algorithm is needed.

cards.title: A directed graph has 1,000 vertices and 3,000 edges (for example, a large network of layers). Store it as an adjacency list or an adjacency matrix?
cards.body:
Adjacency list, because the graph is sparse: only 3,000 of the 1,000,000 possible edges exist.

- Matrix, one byte per entry: $1{,}000 \times 1{,}000 = 1{,}000{,}000$ bytes (about 977 KiB), or 125,000 bytes (about 122 KiB) if each entry is a single bit.
- List in compact form: $3{,}000$ neighbor indices of 2 bytes each plus 1,001 start offsets of 2 bytes each is 8,002 bytes (about 7.8 KiB).

Why: Most matrix entries are zero, and walking a vertex's neighbors means scanning a whole row of 1,000 entries to find perhaps three.

Watch out: The other side: a matrix wins for dense graphs, or when $V$ is tiny. For $V \le 32$ each row fits in one 32-bit word (128 bytes in all), and "is there an edge from $u$ to $v$?" is a single bit test.
